channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: VCs Would Bet on Open-Source AI Over OpenAI and Anthropic | E2341
gist: A This Week in VC panel (Jason Calacanis, Jeff Clavier of Uncork, Jenny Fielding of Everywhere VC, Dave McClure of Practical VC) argues that simultaneous OpenAI/Anthropic price cuts signal a token-selling race to the bottom while open-weight models already carry ~74-78% of routed token volume, so most panelists would bet on open-source/infrastructure (Nvidia, possibly SpaceX) over the frontier labs, which they expect to IPO at 20-30x revenue priced to perfection. They also dissect Instinct's $10B raise as acquisition-underwritten FOMO, seed valuation inflation (median $8M in 2017 to $28M), a buyer's market in private companies outside the top 30, and liquidity tools like continuation SPVs and donor-advised funds.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic shipped new models hours apart and both cut prices sharply: OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna came in about 50% cheaper (Sol at $2 per million tokens), and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 matches Fable 5.1 while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5, with neither being a big capability jump.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Synchronized price cuts without capability jumps point to margin compression at the frontier labs ahead of their IPOs.
insights.quote: neither a big capability jump, but uh both of these are massive price cuts

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier calls frontier-model token selling a race to the bottom in which VC funding subsidizes usage at a loss, making the labs' futures dependent on their ability to keep raising ever-larger rounds.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Lab economics hinge on capital-market access; any funding window closing would hit token pricing and downstream app margins.
insights.quote: Well, it's it's a race to the bottom.

insights.claim: According to token-volume data from an AI routing company shown on the panel, open-weight models account for about 78% of routed token volume versus about 21% for closed-weight models, and open models have held the majority of token usage since roughly Q2 2026 (another figure cited was 74%).
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / panelist
insights.so_what: If open models dominate usage volume, value may accrue to inference infrastructure and routers rather than closed-model API sellers.
insights.quote: open weights open models 78% closed weights 21%

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding would bet on open-source infrastructure over OpenAI and Anthropic, arguing closed labs will 'get crushed' because consumers only care about price and quality and open-source models are close to catching up and face no self-imposed constraints.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: A seed VC openly betting against the two most valuable private AI labs is a sentiment signal ahead of their public listings.
insights.quote: consumers don't care. They just care about price and quality, and they're so close to catching up that we're going to go all open source.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier argues most AI applications do not need the latest frontier-model capabilities, so model routing will push the bulk of workloads to cheaper models, limiting frontier labs' addressable premium usage.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Premium-token demand may be narrower than frontier-lab valuations imply; routing layers gain strategic importance.
insights.quote: Most applications don't need the latest and greatest features of those latest models.

insights.claim: Dave McClure, forced to allocate his own money between open-weight and closed models, would put about 50% into an index of open-weight models and split the rest equally among closed-model labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A diversified barbell across open and closed models is one VC's hedge against uncertainty over which model paradigm wins.
insights.quote: probably 50% index on openweight models and then split my closed models a third, a third, a third between anthropic, open eye, and

insights.claim: A panelist would go 100% into the AI hardware stack because their portfolio startups are all moving to open-source models, and the CEOs of ElevenLabs, Lovable and Figma indicated they are doing the same because they distrust frontier labs that may become competitors.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Large AI-native app companies defecting from frontier APIs to open models would erode lab revenue concentration and favor compute/hardware owners.
insights.quote: They don't trust the Frontier models. They think they're going to be competitors.

insights.claim: A panelist argues that betting on open-weight models is effectively a bet on Nvidia, since there is no single company that captures the open-model field, and suggests SpaceX could become a platform for open-weight models as a second picks-and-shovels play.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: The investable proxy for open-source AI adoption is compute: Nvidia and potentially SpaceX's compute business.
insights.quote: if you're making a bet on Open Wade, you're probably just making a bet on Nvidia, right?

insights.claim: A panelist expects OpenAI and Anthropic to keep growing revenue despite possible margin issues, but flags OpenAI's heavy debt-funded spending commitments as a risk even with Nvidia's Jensen Huang backing it.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: OpenAI's debt load is the weak point to monitor; revenue growth alone may not protect equity or credit holders.
insights.quote: I wonder if OpenAI's, you know, bets on, you know, their spending in the future, which is a lot of debt.

insights.claim: Falling token prices temporarily lift AI startups' margins but also lower barriers to entry, increasing competition; Uncork underwrites investments against the 'true cost of compute' because subsidized pricing could rise 2-5x and turn profitable products upside down.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier / Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Diligence AI app margins at unsubsidized compute prices; cheap tokens are a transient, not a moat.
insights.quote: we try and figure out okay when we invest in something what is the true cost of compute

insights.claim: A panelist predicts Anthropic will go public at a valuation of at least $2-2.5 trillion and OpenAI at about $1.5 trillion, though market-cap growth may slow afterward.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Implies Anthropic priced above OpenAI at IPO, a notable reversal of the private-market pecking order.
insights.quote: Anthropic at least two two and a half trillion and probably OpenAI one and a half trillion

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis warns that frontier-lab IPOs at 20-30x top-line revenue will be priced to perfection and unlikely to be bargains for public-market investors, and Jenny Fielding says she would not advise people to buy them right now.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Early public buyers of AI-lab IPOs may face years of multiple compression before valuations are 'filled in'.
insights.quote: these valuations are 20 to 30 times topline revenue. Jenny, these things will be priced to perfection.

insights.claim: SpaceX's IPO had a major bump, a pullback and then a recovery, with the rebound attributed to a compute business ('Elon Web Services') generating $20-40 billion that did not exist nine months earlier, alongside a Cursor acquisition.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: SpaceX's rapid pivot into AI compute makes it a de facto AI-infrastructure stock; watch compute revenue as the key driver.
insights.quote: that business did not exist 9 months ago

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier wants to own SpaceX but has not bought because it is too expensive, putting his entry price at around $1 trillion market value.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: A veteran VC's buy level well below current SpaceX pricing suggests valuation-sensitive demand sits far lower.
insights.quote: I'm still looking for my entry price in SpaceX. So, I haven't bought SpaceX.

insights.claim: SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to collectively raise more in public markets than all tech companies have raised in the last 45 years, with more than $5 trillion of value involved.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: A supply wave of mega-IPOs could absorb public-market liquidity and pressure other growth equities.
insights.quote: SpaceX, Enthropic and OpenAI will essentially raise in the public market more than all tech companies have raised in the last 45 years.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier says his family office prioritizes capital preservation over risky bets and allocates to more predictable assets such as energy, since his venture work already carries extreme valuation risk.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: VC wealth is rotating toward defensive/real assets like energy rather than doubling down on richly priced tech.
insights.quote: The goal of the family office is to not lose whatever we've made so far.

themes.theme: Instinct $10B raise and consumer AI agents

insights.claim: Instinct, an AI assistant that works through iMessage founded by 23-year-old Noah Shin, went from a seed of $25M at a $50M post-money (April 2026) to a $75M Series A at $500M (August 2026) to a $250M Series B at $2.5B led by Benchmark and Index Ventures, and is reportedly seeking $1B at a $10B valuation with about $350M raised and roughly 100,000 users.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A 20x valuation step-up in months on ~100k users is a marker of peak FOMO in consumer AI agents.
insights.quote: Instinct went from founding to$2.5 billion dollar valuation in under five months.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier is not investing in Instinct because people he knows who used it had a poor experience and stopped over concerns about how much data access it had, and he worries Meta's Muse, the top downloaded app, will crush it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Big-platform assistants with built-in distribution are the main existential risk to standalone consumer agent startups.
insights.quote: if I'm them I'm really worried about news

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding cautions that a fast funding round or markup reflects competitive tension among a small number of funds betting agents are the next platform shift, not proof of a real business.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Discount rapid markups as signals; look for retention and monetization data instead.
insights.quote: just because there's a markup it doesn't really tell you much about the business

insights.claim: Instinct's valuation is being underwritten on a major acquisition by Apple, Amazon, Google or Microsoft, since OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Grok (xAI) already own competing assistants; Apple and Amazon in particular are said to need an agent product they currently lack.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer-agent startups' exit value depends on big-tech acquirers lacking in-house agents; Apple/Amazon agent launches would compress that optionality.
insights.quote: the valuation for Instinct I think people are underwriting a major acquisition.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues that at a $10B valuation Instinct would need a $20B+ acquisition, which pushes potential acquirers like Apple or Microsoft to build rather than buy by paying $10-25M salaries to build it themselves.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Excessive private valuations can kill the M&A exit they are premised on; entry price matters.
insights.quote: at 10 billion you have to be purchased for 20 billion at a minimum

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier reports Instinct is burning so much cash on compute that it needed to raise again only weeks after its last round, while gating access; its founder reportedly does not want to charge users, leaving advertising as the eventual model.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Compute-heavy free consumer agents face structural burn; monetization via ads puts them head-to-head with Meta.
insights.quote: They're burning so much cash on compute that they need to raise

insights.claim: Meta can monetize its Muse assistant through its giant ad network without ever charging users, and its distribution is powerful enough that even a derivative product like Threads reached around 500 million users.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Meta's ad-funded distribution moat is a structural advantage in consumer AI assistants.
insights.quote: there aren't there like 500 million people that use threads? And that's not, you know, a great product

insights.claim: Instinct is compared to Clubhouse, which reached $1B then $4B valuations and reportedly turned down a $4B Twitter acquisition offer before fading, called one of Silicon Valley's biggest mistakes.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Flash-in-the-pan consumer valuations historically reward founders who sell into peak offers.
insights.quote: Twitter offered 4 billion for Clubhouse, I believe was the rumor. They did not take it.

insights.claim: Cursor is cited as evidence that big AI exits exist: it had roughly $2-3B in revenue and was valued at $60B, whereas Instinct has zero revenue and seeks $10B.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Revenue-backed AI exits (Cursor) and pre-revenue raises (Instinct) should not be priced on the same logic.
insights.quote: cursor had two or three billion and they got valued at 60. This has zero and is at 10.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis hears rumors that Google has big frontier-model news and new consumer products coming after holding back out of caution over lawsuits and reputation, and notes Google already has the Gmail, Calendar and Docs data to build a Muse-like assistant.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A Google consumer-agent launch would pressure standalone assistant startups and reset the competitive landscape.
insights.quote: the rumor I'm hearing with Google is big Frontier model news coming and some other consumer products coming

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis's firm abandoned OpenClaw because only three or four technical staff could use it, and adoption jumped to 20-25 people once easier options like Claude Cowork arrived; staff also use Grok, Perplexity and Lovable to build internal software.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Ease of use, not raw power, drives enterprise agent adoption; polished lab products are displacing open-source agent frameworks in small firms.
insights.quote: We gave up on OpenClaw.

themes.theme: AI safety, regulation and trust infrastructure

insights.claim: Dave McClure predicts an AI sovereign-wealth-fund-style deal within 6-12 months in which frontier labs give the government an equity stake in exchange for a product-liability shield, noting Bernie Sanders reportedly wants 50% and Sam Altman offered 5-10%.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A government equity stake or liability shield would materially change frontier-lab dilution and legal risk profiles pre-IPO.
insights.quote: there's going to be a AI fund sovereign wealth fund that'll get cut next year sometime the next 6 to 12 months

insights.claim: A panelist suggests the cigarette-industry settlement is a model for AI regulation, estimating a 10-20% government take and preferring an equity swap over a tax or revenue deal, akin to a Section 230-style shield from hallucination lawsuits.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Frames plausible terms for an AI-industry liability grand bargain investors should model.
insights.quote: I think you can follow sort of the you know the cigarette companies uh you know structure as a very similar model.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier says 26% of Anthropic's next-generation model is being built by AI itself, which he believes makes it increasingly unclear how labs can guarantee safety.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Recursive self-improvement at labs raises tail and regulatory risk that could affect lab valuations.
insights.quote: 26% of Entropic is building, you know, the the next generation of Enthropic

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier cites a reported incident where an AI agent misidentified the cargo of a Chinese ship and the Pentagon nearly intercepted or bombed it before a human stopped it, arguing hallucination makes AI dangerous in military and critical-infrastructure use.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Reliability and human-in-the-loop verification are a growing requirement and investable niche in defense AI.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues AI labs like Anthropic should implement know-your-customer and usage logging for dangerous capabilities, similar to licensed hacking tools like Pegasus, and SendGrid-style tiered usage limits that expand with trust.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: KYC/trust-and-safety layers for AI usage are an emerging compliance category and potential product opportunity.
insights.quote: if Claude's that dangerous, like put in some safeguards, bro.

insights.claim: According to a comment from an OpenRouter investor, Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter was about trust relationships and monitoring untrusted AI token usage rather than lowest-cost routing to open-weight models, because Stripe is fundamentally an anti-fraud company.
insights.speaker: panelist (relaying an OpenRouter investor)
insights.so_what: AI token fraud and abuse detection may become a Stripe-style payments-adjacent moat; watch for trust-layer M&A.
insights.quote: Stripe is not a payments company. Stripe is a anti-fraud company

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding sees cyber and resilience-focused defense tech becoming a massive space, noting a surge of startups working on infrastructure resilience and heavy European focus on sovereignty and defense tech.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Resilience/cyber and sovereign defense tech are high-deal-flow categories for early-stage exposure.
insights.quote: I think like cyber is going to be just this massive space.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis cites MRI studies showing brain activity is lowest when people use AI to write essays and highest when they research and write by hand, warning that over-trust in AI is atrophying human judgment.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Cognitive-atrophy concerns could shape education policy and AI-product design norms.

themes.theme: Seed valuation inflation and fund math

insights.claim: Per a cap-table data provider cited on the panel, median (50th percentile) seed valuations rose from about $8M in 2017 to $28M, the 75th percentile from about $12M to $54M, and the 95th percentile from about $25M to $209M.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: 3.5x median seed inflation means seed investors now need decacorn outcomes for fund-returning results.
insights.quote: 50th percentile was uh 8 million. 50th percentile is now 28.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier explains that with Uncork's $300M fund, a single winner must return about $150M, so a $5-6M seed check needs a 30x at already-high valuations, meaning a multi-billion outcome; unless a company sells for about $10B, seed investors barely make money.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Seed fund returns now depend on rare $10B+ exits; LPs should scrutinize entry prices and ownership targets.
insights.quote: unless you sell something for 10 billion, you barely sort of make money, which is insane

insights.claim: Uncork targets 10-12% ownership in exceptional companies and rarely loses deals except when multi-stage funds write $10-15M seed checks at $100M+ valuations, at which point it bows out.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Multi-stage mega-funds are crowding out traditional seed funds at the top of the market.
insights.quote: come in and write, you know, 10 or $15 million uh seat check at$100 million or more valuation. And at that case, in that case, we just bow out

insights.claim: Seed round norms have shifted dramatically: in 2008 Fitbit's $2M seed at a $5M pre-money was considered massive, 500 Startups' average pre-money in early funds was below $5M, and Jeff Clavier's first seed fund in 2007 was $15M.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier / Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Historical entry prices highlight how compressed forward seed returns are at today's valuations.
insights.quote: Fitbit in 2008 raised a $2 million seed round. It was massive.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says that during the ZIRP-era SaaS peak his firm tried to be a net seller of secondaries to buyers like TPG and Tiger Cubs, and in hindsight should have sold more, implying investors should sell into today's froth.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Suggests taking secondary liquidity on hot AI-era positions now rather than holding for peak marks.
insights.quote: if I could replay that, I would have pushed harder to sell more at that unreasonable peak

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding's Everywhere VC is one of roughly ten remaining firms writing $250K checks into ~$1M B2B pre-seed rounds, a shrinking segment of the market.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Capital scarcity at true pre-seed means better entry prices for the few funds still operating there.
insights.quote: I mean there's like 10 of us left.

themes.theme: Liquidity, exits and the private-market middle

insights.claim: Dave McClure says private-company secondary markets are a seller's market for the top ~30 names (Anthropic, Stripe, Databricks, etc.) but a buyer's market outside them, where companies doing a couple hundred million in revenue, growing 40-50% and profitable lack data and buyers.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Mispricing and bargains exist in private companies ranked ~31-250 for investors who can access financials.
insights.quote: it's a buyer market for a lot of the names that are outside the top 30 if if you know what you're doing

insights.claim: Companies that would have IPO'd 10 years ago at $50-100M in revenue now wait until $500M-$1B, and one unnamed profitable CEO with over $500M revenue told Dave McClure he won't IPO until reaching $10B in revenue, roughly five more years.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Delayed IPOs keep value creation private, raising the importance of secondaries and private-market access.
insights.quote: Not until they're doing 10 billion in revenue.

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier says thousands of venture-backed companies are stuck in the middle, and when Bending Spoons buys companies making $400-500M in revenue at about 2x revenue, investors see their last-round marks written down 80-90%.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Late-stage marks in stalled growth companies are likely overstated; PE-style acquirers set the real floor.
insights.quote: Those companies are getting written down by 80 to 90% from their last round mark.

insights.claim: Uncork's exit of DroneDeploy, an investment made 13 years earlier, returned half of the fund to investors, and Uncork has sold about $1.5B worth of portfolio companies in the last three to four months after a roughly five-year pause.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Early-stage AI-era M&A is reopening, a leading indicator of improving VC DPI.
insights.quote: we've sold about $1.5 billion worth of stuff in the last three, four months, which hasn't happened for a while

insights.claim: Dave McClure proposes a 'single asset continuity SPV': within 3-6 months after a Series B or C, a fund sells part of a winner into an SPV at that round's post-money price, generating DPI in years five to eight while LPs can choose liquidity or roll into the new vehicle.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A replicable GP-led liquidity tool for emerging managers struggling to show DPI.
insights.quote: You can use the post money price on that round as a legitimate objective transfer price for the asset from your initiating fund to an SPV.

insights.claim: Dave McClure recommends donating illiquid assets such as startup stock, GP/LP fund interests or carried interest to a donor-advised fund that accepts them to get an immediate deduction at third-party fair market value, usable against taxes for the current year and up to five years forward, with a roughly 30-day process that must be done by December.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Tax planning tool for holders of illiquid or busted-unicorn equity and employees with 2026 secondary liquidity.
insights.quote: instead of you know donating your cash you should really be donating the assets that you haven't already been taxed on

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis's team is building 'Twist 100', a community-tracked list of the top 100 private companies with latest prices, while Practical VC similarly rehosts the top ~40 names using Augment's numbers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Demand for private-market pricing data and ranking tools is growing as companies stay private longer.

insights.claim: Web 2.0-era exits like Weblogs Inc.'s $30M sale to AOL at roughly 300x revenue ($125K revenue) returned Mark Cuban about $5M on a $300K investment in under 18 months; panelists say similar early acquisitions are returning in the AI era but at higher entry prices.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) / Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Early acqui-style exits can produce strong multiples only when entry prices are low.

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding reports a fintech-healthcare portfolio company at about $3M ARR, built on a $2M pre-seed, could not raise a Series A because investors disliked its margins, category and non-hypergrowth, and is instead bridging with a ~$3M seed led by insiders; the founder believes a Series A would have closed 18 months ago.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Non-AI fintech/healthcare Series A capital is scarce, creating potential value entry points for contrarian investors.
insights.quote: the founder even said 18 months ago I would have gotten a series A done

insights.claim: Jeff Clavier says 'triple triple double double double' growth that guaranteed financing three to four years ago no longer gets attention, making round timing and sizing harder than ever to predict except for clear breakout companies.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Solid-but-not-AI-hypergrowth companies face a funding gap; founders should raise opportunistically.
insights.quote: if you show up with a triple triple double double double which guaranteed you uh financing three four years ago right now nobody cares

insights.claim: An Uncork portfolio company growing quickly to tens of millions in revenue announced a $100M Series C from Insight Partners.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Growth capital remains available for clear revenue breakouts even as middle-tier rounds dry up.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis's founder heuristic: if the valuation is good, the investor is good and the terms are clean, take the money; he cites Micro1, which he backed at a $12M valuation, reaching hundreds of millions in revenue, being profitable and raising $100M at a $4B valuation, with his firm owning about 6%.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: AI training-data vendors like Micro1 are producing outsized, profitable outcomes for early backers.
insights.quote: good valuation, good investor, clean terms, just effing do it

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis bought additional Robinhood shares in the public market at $8-9 when he judged the stock mispriced, and it now trades above $100, making him a larger holder than when it was private.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Post-IPO drawdowns in venture-backed fintech can offer asymmetric public-market entries.
insights.quote: I bought a bunch at $8 or $9 now over $100 a share.

insights.claim: Loft Orbital, a shared-satellite-missions company, announced a $1B investment from Abu Dhabi for a constellation Jeff Clavier says will be the largest AI compute constellation in space, running AI models on orbit so customers receive actionable results instead of multi-gigabyte images.
insights.speaker: Jeff Clavier
insights.so_what: Orbital AI compute is attracting sovereign capital; a theme alongside SpaceX's compute push.
insights.quote: which will be the largest AI compute constellation in space

insights.claim: TaxGPT, a Founder University graduate that later went through Y Combinator, has reached tens of millions of dollars in revenue with thousands of tax and accounting firms using it.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Vertical AI for accounting is scaling fast, a sign of durable demand in professional-services AI.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis's firm uses internally built AI tooling over 20,000 funding applications to identify companies it met but passed on that later raised a Series B, then targets them for its syndicate to make up for missed investments such as Zipline.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: AI-driven 'missed deal' analysis is a practical way for VCs to recapture exposure to breakout companies in later rounds.
insights.quote: We're doing the misses. So, we missed Zipline 10 years ago.
